Online Petscam

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Thousands of people world-wide are being lured into an on-line pedigree pet buying scam, and South Africans are also being targeted, we expose the scammers.

Unique Selling Point:
We have received more than 40 websubs over a two year period from viewers who have fallen victim to the on-line pet scam phenomenon. It's a worldwide problem, and scammers are able to lure innocent buyers, looking for pedigree pets like English Bulldogs or Maine Coon kittens, into parting with their hard earned money through a sophisticated scam. Their websites look authentic, but in the meantime the animals put up for sale never actually exist, and the photos of the pets for sale have been stolen from actual breeders or online sellers.

Further information:
We have two active cell phone nrs being used by scammers who we will try to track down
We have a server host/internet cafe in Braamfontein called Click View who are hosting a lot of the scammers who we will try to confront

Script:


Online Petscam
24 October 2019
First Draft

Voice
For many South Africans, pets are extended members of the family - filling our homes with joy and companionship.

Link Masa
But buyer, beware. Many websites offering pedigreed pets for sale may look upmarket and legit, but the reality is they are nothing more than window dressing setup by sophisticated scammers looking to con you out of your hard earned cash.

Voice
Rensche Esterhuizen from the East Rand says she searched the web a few months ago for a puppy as a gift for her brother.

Sound Up Rensche
So I found this website puppies4southafrica specifically, where I was looking at different types of puppies and sending photos to my brother and asking him which one he would like, and then he said ok no he wants the corgi.

Voice
Impressed by the professional presentation, Esterhuizen contacted Puppies4Southafrica.

Sound Up Rensche
Masa: do you have a vet, where are you located? I mean this makes you think they really care right?

Rensche: Exactly.

Voice
In actual fact, the questions are just STEP ONE of the scam - the fraudsters want to know where you live, because in their next response to you, they’ll say they are somewhere on the other side of the country.

Sound Up Rensche
They said they’re from Swellendam, they want a nice and safe home, you must insure that you’re not a breeder.

Voice
The scammers don’t want you to come and see the pet, and they’re going to charge you an extra fee for a courier.

Sound Up Rensche
The puppy was R2500, but then plus R500 to get it delivered to me.

Voice
This Johannesburg resident, who has asked us not to use her real name, came across a scam site while looking for two Pomeranians she wanted to buy for her children.

Sound Up “Jewel.”
Then I said ok, can we come see the puppies - and then came the oh no, we’re not in Johannesburg, we are in an outlying town.

Voice
In both cases the scammers wanted a deposit upfront to “secure” the sale of the pet.


Sound Up “Jewel”
They asked for the full amount upfront, and then they said they would ship it to my home address.

Voice
Esterhuizen paid her deposit, and was then lured into STEP TWO of the scam - the victim is required to pay a whole slew of extra costs.

Sound Up Rensche
Then they started no but another R3000 for the cage, because it’s a special cage that it needs to come into and another R3000 for some pet insurance.

Voice
Jewel realised she was being scammed and never paid a cent. But Esterhuizen lost thousands, and her promised puppy never arrived.

Sound Up Rensche
Rensche: And only after 6 o clock on the friday evening, when they said the dog would have arrived, I realised this was a big scam.

Voice
The enticing photos used for petscams are often stolen from elsewhere on the web, as was the case with this image from the puppies4southafrica website.

Sound Up Masa
We found this cute labrador on this fake site called Tom, did a reverse image search and it turns out that Tom is the puppy of the Junior Champion of Bulgaria.

Voice
We posed as a potential buyer and received an almost exact replica of the response Esterhuizen got from puppies4southafrica, supposedly from a woman named Gail.

Sound Up Rensche
Masa: They all have a great personality, all kid friendly, I mean verbatim. So they obviously copy and paste and send it to everyone.

Voice
But once we revealed we were journalists, Gail refused to answer our calls.

Sound Up Massa
Voicemail: You don’t need to leave a message

Masa: Oh, we don’t need to leave a message.

Voice
It’s a global problem. Steven Baker is the US based Better Business Bureau’s International Investigations Specialist.

Sound Up Steve Baker
I did a deep dive into puppy frauds we have in the US and Canada, we have tens of thousands of complaints about puppy frauds. At one point we believed that 80% of the sponsored links that appeared on the top of search engines, were really going to fraudsters.

Link Masa
At some point the victim realises that they’ve been scammed, and will stop giving over any money. And you would think that’s where their troubles end, but you’d be wrong.

Voice
Luzanne Erasmus from the Western Cape found her dream pet, a Ragdoll kitten, on a petscam website called Ronelleskittens.

Sound Up Luzanne
And then I got an email from a woman called Helga, sending me photos of Ragdoll kittens, and yes I decided to take one of these kittens.

Voice
Erasmus was conned into STEP THREE of the scam - Identity theft. The scammers, pretending to be a woman named Helga Jansen van Rensburg, sent Erasmus a copy of the real Helga’s ID as security for the deposit she had to pay. They also asked her for a copy of her ID - supposedly to register her pet.

Sound Up
Masa: So you ended up giving a copy of your ID?

Luzanne: I did yes.

Voice
And just like that Erasmus had unwittingly become the victim of identity theft, just like the real Helga had been earlier this year when she was conned in a puppy scam.

Sound Up Helga
Then I received a call from a captain at Stellenbosch police department and they phoned me and said are you aware of the fraud case that’s been opened up against you? And I was like, for what? And they said well you sold them a dog, or a puppy, and you took their money so they’ve opened up a case against you.

Voice
The scammers were fraudulently using Helga’s name and ID to rip off more and more victims. She even came onto our radar as several Carte Blanche viewers, wrongfully believing her to be the scammer submitted their stories to us. She says the nightmare reached fever pitch when she was named and shamed on Facebook.

Sound Up Helga
First of all, my photo on my Facebook was of my son, so my son was exposed, that completely devastated me.

Voice
Luzanne Erasmus was able to have her bank reverse the deposit she’d paid, but having heard the truth about Helga, she now worries that she might be next. (die vanne hierso maak mens actually bietjie deurmekaar…ek het gedink Helga maak dit net duidelik as ons by haar naam jou hier)

Sound Up Luzanne
They’ve got my email, ja I even sent them the google maps with the location directly to my house.

Voice
Pet scams are essentially an evolution of the well-known “419” or “advance fee fraud” scams. This man, whom we’ll call Hector, is a member of an international organisation called Artists Against 419 that works with law enforcement agencies worldwide to bring the fraudsters to book, so he’s asked us to hide his identity.

Sound Up “Hector”
Masa: Please explain to me, what is advanced fee fraud?

Hector: Advance fee fraud is basically where you will be paying money upfront for a service, or a product, or even a promise, and then getting defrauded.

Voice
Both Artists Against 419 and the Better Business Bureau say that while the origins of the 419 scam can be traced to Nigeria, pet scams evolved in Cameroon.

Sound Up Steve
This seems to be a Cameroonian specialty, we know that for a couple of ways. First of all there have been some arrests in the United States of people running puppy scams, and they’re all Cameroonian students who’ve come here on student visas.

Voice
Tracking down the fraudsters behind each individual site is nearly impossible - but with Artists Against 419’s help we were able to identify a company called Vitalclick Technologies, which among other services, provides internet hosting. We identified no less than 28 alleged scam sites hosted by Vitalclick’s name servers - amongst them 3 pet scams. According to the CIPC’s database their registered address was at this Internet Cafe in Johannesburg CBD.

Sound Up Masa
We’ve found the location of an internet cafe in downtown joburg that’s hosting some of these scammers sites, we really don’t know what to expect, so we’ve taken a little extra security as we head out there.

Voice
The address led us to the inner city, and the first floor office of this dodgy looking building. Inside we found a man who told us his name was Martin.

Sound Up Martin

Masa: We’re looking for the owners of Vital Click, or the managers?

Martin: This is not Vital Click.

Masa:Oh it’s not Vital Click?

Martin: Ja.

Masa: What is it called?

Martin: There is no name.

Masa: Oh, it doesn’t have a name?

Martin: Ja.

Voice
Martin said his unnamed shop was no longer an internet cafe and only offered photocopying facilities. And he claimed not to know Vitalclick director Anthony Abi-da-kun.

Sound Up Martin
Martin: Me, I’m from Cameroon, and that name seems like a nigerian name.

Link Masa
Well, elusive once again, they claim that the internet cafe has moved and they don’t know the previous owners - we don’t know.

Voice
But our producers did manage to get hold of Anthony Abi-da-kun. HE said they had moved from downtown Jo and that he was unavailable for an on-camera interview prior to our broadcast date.

Sound Up Anthony Abidakun
Producer: I have information here that about 28 websites, that are hosted by Vitalclick, on your name servers, are scams?

Anthony: Ja, whenever we receive any reports, we shut down websites, that’s what we do. And we contact the owner, there’s a report of a website, can you please explain yourself?

Producer: And if I was to send you my list of information, the sites that I know are being hosted by you that I believe are fraudulent, would you be willing to take them down?

Anthony: Definitely.

Voice
In the deceptive world of pet scams, our experts say there is one bulletproof way of protecting yourself from becoming a victim: if you can’t see it, touch it, and bring it home for yourself, don’t pay for it.
